transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-12
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Ravi (Redwood CSM), Samir (Aurelia platform), Lisa (Aurelia security), Tom (Aurelia SRE), Priya (Aurelia PM)

Summary (auto): Weekly POC sync for Redwood Private VPC pilot. Reviewed latest throughput/latency numbers from on-prem test cluster, discussed VPC routing anomalies, NAT gateway timeouts, and kernel/driver upgrades required on the customer's GPU hosts. Agreed next steps: share network diagram, gather flow logs, apply iptables tweaks and kernel params, and run isolated throughput test.

[00:00] Maya: Hey all, thanks for joining — we'll do a quick check-in on the private pilot, focus on networking and the small upgrade we recommended. How's everyone?
[00:12] Samir: Good, thanks. Been heads down with the install, had a couple of odd routing results after we applied the early config.
[00:20] Jordan: Cool. We pulled the runbook changes into the test cluster and ran two 1-hour runs overnight — I'll share the raw logs after. Quick overview — throughput looks fine except for bursts where connections were being reset, which points at the NAT/timewait thresholds on the bastion layer.
[00:37] Tom: Yeah, we've seen resets at ~P95 of concurrent connections, roughly when the model cache was doing a heavy KV prefetch. The worker kernels also logged timeouts during checkpointing.
[00:47] Lisa: From a security standpoint we want to avoid opening broad ephemeral ranges; any networking fix has to be compatible with our firewall policy.
[00:55] Jordan: Understood. In the run we saw connection churn when the control plane tried to re-route to a fallback model variant — that triggered more outbound connections than expected. Two areas: ephemeral port exhaustion on the NAT (we think) and slightly aggressive TCP keepalive settings on the nodes.
[01:12] Samir: We have AWS-like NAT Gateway behavior in our VPC appliance, but it's a private appliance (not AWS-managed). It limits ephemeral ports a bit differently. We can increase ephemeral range, but want to know the recommended range.
[01:24] Jordan: Recommendation is to expand the ephemeral range to 32768-61000 and increase net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range accordingly, and also bump net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse and tcp_fin_timeout to 30s from default 60s to reduce TIME_WAIT accumulation. We'll put an exact snippet in the notes.
[01:40] Priya: Quick question — will that change impact other services in the VPC? We don't want to break our telemetry or EHR connections.
[01:49] Jordan: It should be limited, but Samir should test in a dev subnet first. We can also scope the change to the inference subnet via iptables NAT translation rules.
[01:59] Samir: Ok we'll test.
[02:05] Maya: On the higher level, we also recommended a kernel/driver stack upgrade on the GPU hosts to address a jittery driver behavior that can cause small stalls. Samir, what's your timeline for performing OS-level upgrades?
[02:16] Samir: We prefer a maintenance window next weekend, but we need the exact kernel version and the driver notes. We did see one kernel oops last week during heavy batch inference.
[02:24] Jordan: The versions we validated are Ubuntu 22.04 with kernel 5.15.x backports and NVIDIA driver 525.x or newer. There's a small patch set for the NVIDIA MIG/driver handshake we applied in our lab. We'll share those patch notes. Note: you may need to coordinate with your hardware vendor for certified driver bundles.
[02:41] Tom: Is there any risk that the upgrade will break our quantized runtime? We run int8 profiles for cost reasons.
[02:49] Jordan: We've run quantized models through the same driver stack in our internal lab and didn't see regressions. The main item is the CUDA/cuDNN compatibility matrix — we'll list exact tested combos.
[02:57] Lisa: Also need to confirm that the private control plane still can rotate keys via KMS after the upgrade.
[03:02] Maya: Good point. Lisa, can you remind us the KMS provider?
[03:06] Lisa: We're on a managed HSM via our cloud partner, key ARNs follow the pattern arn:cloud:keys:... I'll share the exact ARN offline. Need to ensure Redwood can call Encrypt/Decrypt for the node bootstrap role.
[03:19] Jordan: On that — Redwood Private's bootstrap uses short-lived certs for the node and then the control plane requests keys for model artifacts and cache encryption. We can use a customer-managed key; we support IAM role assumption and HSM flows. We'll attach sample policy.
[03:31] Maya: Switching to results — Jordan, can you run through the latency/throughput summary?
[03:36] Jordan: Sure. From last night's 1-hour run: average p50 generation latency was 110ms per 512-token step on the small test model, p95 spiked to 420ms during cache miss storms; tokens/sec averaged 1.8k across the pool with sustained bursts up to 2.4k, but we saw errors climb from 0.2% to 1.5% during the spike window. The errors were mostly connection resets and a handful of grpc deadline exceeded from the control plane.
[04:02] Samir: The 1.5% error corresponds to the time our VPC appliance logged 503-style responses due to session table limits.
[04:10] Jordan: Exactly. Two mitigations: increase ephemeral range / tcp params, and add a lightweight local proxy on the worker nodes to pool and reuse connections to the control plane — that'll cut the churn. We can provide a sidecar config for that proxy.
[04:25] Priya: Sounds good. Any recommended tolerances for SLA during pilot? We're trying to define success criteria.
[04:32] Maya: For pilot, suggested acceptance is <1% error and p95 latency under 500ms for 512-token steps under typical traffic profile. If we hit those after the network changes and N days of stability (we usually ask 72h), we consider moving to canary rollout.
[04:46] Tom: Can we also get a breakdown per-model? Some of our load is from a long-form summarization model that behaves differently.
[04:53] Jordan: Yes — we'll push the per-model metrics. The long-form one has larger KV cache and higher memory pressure, which increases reclaims and GC events; that aligns with the times we saw spikes.
[05:06] Samir: About routing — we observed that when we intentionally moved a model route to a fallback variant (smaller quantized model) the routing sometimes didn't prefer the closest AZ instance and instead chose a more distant node, increasing cross-AZ latency.
[05:21] Jordan: That's likely due to our early topology hints not matching your VPC's AZ tagging. We use an internal affinity score (latency + cost) but if AZ labels are missing or ambiguous the routing may fall back to a different heuristic.
[05:34] Samir: How hard is it to enforce AZ-awareness?
[05:37] Jordan: Not hard — need one thing: consistent zone tags on instances and a simple route table annotation for affinity. We'll provide a small script to annotate and a routing policy tweak.
[05:46] Lisa: From compliance, we need explicit mention of cross-AZ data residency for certain workloads.
[05:51] Maya: We'll include a routing policy doc that describes data-in-motion boundaries and how to pin routes to AZ/local-host-only.
[05:59] Tom: Another observation — after a minor upgrade to our Open vSwitch rules we saw some ARP flaps; could that be related to the high frequency of ephemeral connections?
[06:08] Jordan: It could amplify churn but ARP flaps usually indicate missed gratuitous ARP or proxy ARP misconfig. We can help inspect the VPC appliance logs.
[06:16] Samir: We'll attach the logs.
[06:19] Jordan: Great. On the software side we recommended enabling prefix/KV caching on a longer TTL for responses that are safe to cache. That reduces burst startup traffic.
[06:29] Priya: Any risk to model freshness with longer TTLs?
[06:33] Jordan: For most generation tasks it's fine; for data-sensitive or frequently changing prompt templates we can set shorter TTL and apply cache invalidation hooks. We'll document patterns.
[06:42] Maya: Okay, let's capture next steps — Jordan will send the iptables/sysctl snippets and sidecar proxy config; Samir will supply VPC flow logs and run the dev-subnet test; Lisa to confirm KMS ARN and policy; Maya will update pilot scope and pricing with an optional Dedicated fallback and timeline.
[06:59] Samir: One more ask — any quick wins we can apply without kernel upgrades?
[07:03] Jordan: Yes: ephemeral range/tw_reuse, add the local proxy sidecar, and limit canary fanout in the control plane to avoid wide fanout on route changes. Those are low risk.
[07:15] Lisa: We'll want an internal change window for the proxy deploy.
[07:19] Maya: We'll coordinate schedules.
[07:22] Ravi: From onboarding, we'll also prepare a short runbook for your ops team that lists rollback steps if the upgrade causes regressions.
[07:30] Priya: That'd be great.
[07:33] Maya: Any blockers?
[07:34] Samir: None we can't handle; just need the exact config snippets and a little time to run the dev subnet tests.
[07:41] Maya: Perfect. We'll follow up with artifacts by 02/14. Thanks everyone.
